summary: Discovery focused on per-token economics and deployment tradeoffs. Pulse AI is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for cost predictability and data controls. Agreed next steps: send pricing + security docs and run a benchmark pilot with sample prompts.
topics: Per-token pricing and example cost calculations
KV/prefix caching and cache hit impact on unit cost
transcript:
[00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro - I'm Ava, AE on the Redwood team. Marcus is our systems engineer.
[00:12] Elena Park: Hi all, Elena here, Head of ML at Pulse AI. Tom and Ravi on from infra. We're mainly here to understand cost, latency, and options - hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:22] Tom Bishop: We've been running some internal prompts against open models and costs are spiking. looking for better cost predictability and maybe move away from fully self-hosted.
[00:30] Marcus Lee: Cool. high level, Redwood offers Hosted API for quick start, Dedicated reserved pools for predictability and Private (VPC/on-prem) for data control. For economics, we usually break down per-token pricing and the operational levers: batching, prefix/KV cache, and quantization.
[00:46] Ravi Shah: Can you give a concrete example? like per 1k tokens how does hosted compare to dedicated?
[00:53] Ava Martinez: Sure - ballpark examples we shared in the deck: hosted list price for an Llama-family-ish model variant is X per 1k prompt tokens and Y per 1k completion tokens - for discussion let's say roughly $0.06 per 1k tokens end-to-end on hosted depending on model. Dedicated is lower unit cost once you commit because you amortize the GPU pool - that can be 30-60% less per token depending on utilization and model.
[01:20] Elena Park: those percentages are big, what's driving it?
[01:23] Marcus Lee: utilization, batching, and caching. Dedicated lets you set aggressive batching and concurrent request patterns. Also we run optimizations and quantized kernels on the runtime; with 4-bit quantization you get ~1.5x-2x token throughput which lowers cost. But that's model dependent and some regen of quality might happen - need evals.
[01:41] Tom Bishop: Our biggest worry is latency. we have some user-facing features with 300ms p95 targets. can batching break that?
[01:49] Marcus Lee: good question. there's a tradeoff. continuous batching helps throughput and cost, but adds queuing latency. Redwood's runtime supports latency-aware routing so you can reserve a latency pool (small batch sizes) for low-latency calls and a throughput pool (bigger batches) for background calls. Also prefix/KV cache reduces tokens needed for the model: if you have repeated prefixes, cache hits can reduce compute by 40-80% for certain workflows.
[02:14] Ravi Shah: Is KV cache a managed thing? where does the cache live and how does it affect billing?
[02:18] Marcus Lee: yes, it's built into the serving runtime. cache is per-customer and can be local to the GPU serving stack; for Dedicated and Private you control retention. Billing: we meter actual tokens processed by the runtime; if cache hits reduce decoded/computed tokens, your billed tokens go down. We show effective cost per served token after cache in our runbooks.
[02:39] Elena Park: can you walk through a worked example - say we serve 10M tokens/month with 40% cache hit and average length 150 tokens.
[02:47] Ava Martinez: quick calc - 10M tokens raw, 40% cache hit => 6M billed tokens. At $0.06 per 1k tokens that's (6,000 * 0.06) = $360. But that number is illustrative; Dedicated could drop that to $0.025 per 1k when amortized with good utilization. so same effective billed tokens but lower unit price.
[03:14] Tom Bishop: that $360 seems off vs our current bills, maybe their base numbers are different.
[03:17] Ava Martinez: yeah these are illustrative; we'll send a detailed pricing sheet with model buckets. Also note embeddings and other ops have different pricing.
[03:25] Ravi Shah: what about quantization - does Redwood support 4-bit and does that change output quality?
[03:29] Marcus Lee: we support quantized model variants; our compilation layer picks kernels. 4-bit usually reduces compute cost significantly but you must validate for your prompts. We recommend running an eval set during pilot. Quality regressions are model and prompt dependent.
[03:44] Elena Park: Pilot - what does that look like? we want to run 200k tokens/day for two weeks to measure costs and p95 latency.
[03:51] Marcus Lee: sounds good. typical pilot: we provision a small Dedicated pool or run on Hosted with an instrumented trace. We collect token counts, cache hit rates, batch size distributions, and latency percentiles. For Dedicated pilot we can provide a discounted reserved trial to simulate committed pricing.
[04:09] Tom Bishop: private deployment - we have compliance needs around residency and KMS. Is Private fully air-gapped?
[04:16] Ava Martinez: Private can be VPC-hosted or on-prem. For on-prem we can package the control plane as customer-managed; KMS/HSM integrations are supported. We'll share our SOC 2 / encryption / audit log docs.
[04:28] Ravi Shah: what's the effort to move from Hosted to Dedicated? downtime?
[04:31] Marcus Lee: migration is mostly config and routing. you can start on Hosted, then reserve Dedicated capacity and shift traffic with canary. Redwood supports A/B rollouts and automatic fallbacks. No major downtime expected.
[04:42] Elena Park: how do you handle fallbacks if Dedicated is saturated?
[04:45] Marcus Lee: smart routing - route to Hosted or a cheaper variant automatically. you can set policies by latency/cost/region.
[04:52] Tom Bishop: procurement question - do you do monthly commit pricing or annual?
[04:56] Ava Martinez: both. Dedicated usually prefers monthly or annual reserved commitments with sliding scale discounts. Hosted remains usage-based. We'll include model-band pricing and examples.
[05:04] Ravi Shah: any gotchas on network egress or data transfer?
[05:07] Marcus Lee: if you're running Private on-prem or in customer VPC, egress is internal. For Hosted we recommend co-locating in same cloud region to minimize network latency and egress costs - we'll include region guidance.
[05:18] Elena Park: what about tooling to monitor per-route token costs?
[05:21] Ava Martinez: Redwood Console shows per-route per-token breakdowns, token cost, latency histograms, and traces. You can tag routes and get cost allocation.
[05:30] Tom Bishop: can we set hard budget caps per route?
[05:33] Marcus Lee: yes, quotas and rate limiting are supported; also automated cost alerts.
[05:36] Elena Park: one more thing - our ML team wants deterministic performance for model evaluations. do you support pinning model versions and reproducible runtimes?
[05:44] Marcus Lee: yes; both Hosted and Dedicated allow model version pinning and we snapshot models and runtime configs for evals.
[05:51] Tom Bishop: ok let's recap next steps.
[05:54] Ava Martinez: recap: we'll send pricing sheet and Dedicated sizing, SOC2/encryption docs, and a pilot proposal. Marcus will lead the technical pilot and set up benchmarks. Pulse to send sample prompts, current monthly token volumes, and latency SLOs.
[06:08] Elena Park: sounds good. thanks.
[06:10] Tom Bishop: thanks everybody.
[06:12] Ava Martinez: I'll follow up with calendar invites for the technical deep dive and the pilot.
[06:17] [call ends]

Notes: transcription has typical ASR noise - a few product names transcribed oddly (e.g., "Redwood Dedicate" for Dedicated). Pricing examples in call are illustrative; final pricing will be provided in follow-up.
